references.text: Also here in Luke, a "only" (μονογενής) son is mentioned – the widow's only son in Nain. Luke uses this word to emphasize the deep sorrow of losing one's only child.
Again, Luke uses the term μονογενής for an only child – a man asks Jesus for help with his only son who is possessed. The parallel shows Jesus' care for families at risk of losing their only child.
The word μονογενής is also used for God's only Son in John 3:16, showing the theological depth of the term – it concerns what is unique and most precious.
Mark's parallel account about Jairus and his daughter. Mark tells of the synagogue leader who comes to Jesus and asks him to come and lay hands on his dying daughter.
Matthew's parallel account about Jairus' daughter. Matthew recounts the same event, but with somewhat fewer details.
The context immediately before: Jesus returns and the crowd welcomes him, and Jairus, a synagogue leader, falls at Jesus' feet and asks him to come to his home.
Also in Mark's account, the crowding of the crowd (ὄχλος) pressing around Jesus is described, parallel to how the crowds "pressed upon him" (συνέπνιγον) in Luke.
Zacchaeus could not see Jesus because of the crowd – another example in Luke where large crowds surround Jesus and create obstacles.
